stories.headline: UN warns of ethnic cleansing as Israel squeezes space in Gaza
body: The United Nations human rights office (OHCHR) warned on Friday that Israeli forces are deepening the displacement of Palestinians in Gaza, raising concerns of ethnic cleansing. The OHCHR said Israel has stated its aim to expand its military deployment area to 70 percent of Gaza’s territory, pushing Palestinians into an ever-shrinking fraction of the besieged enclave.

Over the past two weeks, the OHCHR documented the westward expansion of Israeli military deployment in Al Shujaiyeh, Gaza City, and in eastern Al Bureij, eastern Deir Al-Balah and eastern Al Maghazi in central Gaza. The Israeli army is encroaching past its so-called “Yellow Line” demarcation boundary, and the OHCHR said Israeli forces appear to treat that line as a kill zone, preventing Palestinians from returning to what remains of their homes on the other side.

In Al Shujaiyeh, at least two Israeli attacks were reported on displacement camps, and forces reportedly used explosive robots to detonate the few buildings left standing. The OHCHR said it received reports that on 25 October an Israeli drone dropped munitions on tents sheltering displaced families at the Al Shujaiyeh junction near the Yellow Line, causing a fire that burned for five hours. According to the Palestinian Ministry of Public Works and Housing, the attack displaced 200 families comprising 800 people, mostly women, children and older persons.

Ajith Sunghay, head of the OHCHR in the Occupied Palestinian Territory, described the displacement nightmare as both acute and chronic. “Those displaced before the announcement of a ceasefire have little to no prospect of return to the areas they fled, most of which are inaccessible because they fall beyond the so-called yellow line. And they continue to be displaced again and again,” he said. The OHCHR stressed that as an occupying power, Israel must cease the forcible transfer of Palestinians within Gaza, a war crime that may also amount to a crime against humanity, and must facilitate safe and dignified return.

Despite a ceasefire that took effect on 11 October 2025, Israeli attacks on Gaza have continued. The enclave’s Ministry of Health reports at least 1,574 people killed and 5,687 wounded since the ceasefire began, with total casualties since October 2023 reaching at least 74,570 killed and 175,808 wounded. The displacement crisis is worsened by Israeli restrictions on the entry of shelter-related humanitarian aid, leaving many facing a fourth winter in flimsy tents while still under fire. “Let this be the last,” Sunghay said.

stories.headline: Ship fire off Oman stokes Iran-US escalation fears; oil prices jump more than 2%
body: A ship was reported on fire in the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday, the British maritime agency UKMTO said, as Iran reported shooting down another US drone and oil prices jumped more than 2% on renewed supply fears. The UKMTO, run by the British Royal Navy, said a captain had reported a blaze onboard a vessel spotted 9 nautical miles (17 kilometers) north of the town of Khasab in Oman, just off the strait. The agency gave no details on the cause, any casualties, or the status of the crew, and no information has emerged on damage or environmental impact.

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said in a statement on Thursday that three tankers had exploded and caught fire in the past 24 hours after hitting sea mines while using an "unauthorized" route. It is not known whether the case reported to the UKMTO is one of them. On Friday, the IRGC Navy said it had halted two tankers in the strait's southern waters - one in the eastern part and one in the western part - after they attempted to pass through an unauthorized route, switched off their navigation and positioning systems, and ignored several radio warnings. The IRGC accused the US military of supporting the attempted passage and blamed what it called hostile US actions, along with the vessels' disregard for Iranian regulations, for the incidents and fires aboard the ships. It also said another vessel that caught fire in the strait's southern waters on Thursday night had sunk.

The incidents are part of a broader escalation since the Middle East war was triggered in February by US and Israeli attacks on Iran. Tehran has sought to control the strait, a key transit point for global oil and natural gas supplies, and has attacked ships it considers unauthorized users. Oil exports through the waterway fell again last week, according to shipping data provider Kpler, and attacks on ships in the strait are at their highest level since the war began, according to the US-based Washington Institute for Near East Policy. The US Navy, which is enforcing its own blockade of Iranian vessels, has recently escorted tankers through the strait in the same area where the burning ship was reportedly sighted.

The reported ship fire coincided with Iran's claim that its forces downed another US drone near the strait. The Tasnim news agency cited the IRGC as saying a new, advanced air defense system was used, and that Iran's armed forces have destroyed 14 drones of this type and more than 50 MQ-9 Reaper drones since the war broke out. The claims have not been independently verified, though the US Congressional Research Service says dozens of US aircraft and drones have been reported lost or damaged since the war began.

The latest developments come as US President Donald Trump is widely seen as considering fresh strikes against Iran after the US midterm elections on November 3. Last week, Trump said "we may do another little Epic Fury," referring to the US-Israeli attacks on Tehran in February that triggered the war, though he gave no timeframe. A third US aircraft carrier and thousands of additional troops are currently heading to the region. As reports of a possible renewed escalation circulate, US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has reportedly fired the Pentagon's top military planner, Army Lieutenant General Brett Sylvia. If confirmed, it would be the latest in a series of high-level departures under the Trump administration; Sylvia's predecessor, Lieutenant General Joseph McGee, was forced to retire last October. According to a report in The Atlantic, no reason was given for Sylvia's departure and no replacement has been named.

stories.headline: Tech stocks rout deepens as AI capex fears erase over $1 trillion
stories.byline: Financial & Markets desk · anchored on Reuters
body: US technology stocks suffered a severe sell-off on Friday as investors recoiled from mounting evidence that Big Tech’s massive spending on artificial intelligence is not yet translating into commensurate profits. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite opened at its lowest level in more than two months, falling more than 2%, while the S&P 500 also fell. The declines were led by Intel, which plunged as much as 30% after warning of a prolonged PC slowdown, and Amazon, which fell as much as 6% after reporting that its free cash flow had swung to a record negative outflow of more than $42 billion over the past 12 months, driven by a more than doubling of capital spending on data centers and equipment in the third quarter.

The earnings season has laid bare the tension between AI ambitions and financial discipline. Alphabet lost more than $500 billion in market value on Thursday after revealing that its AI-generated search summaries were cannibalizing core advertising revenue; its shares fell another 1% on Friday. Amazon’s spending on property and equipment reached about $77 billion from July through September, more than double the $35 billion a year earlier, while its operations generated only about $42 billion in cash, leaving a roughly $33 billion gap over three months. Intel’s finance chief David Zinsner said the company did not expect to generate positive free cash flow this year and forecast lower-than-expected fourth-quarter revenue, adding that the PC slowdown would likely persist through the first half of next year. The sell-off also hit social media and gaming stocks: Reddit tumbled 24% after reporting weaker-than-expected daily active users and warning that Google’s AI-driven search was hurting referral traffic; Roblox fell 16% after its daily active users dropped 9% year over year; and Pinterest declined 6% after missing revenue and earnings estimates.

The rout hit the Magnificent Seven hard: Meta and Alphabet are effectively in bear markets—down more than 20% from their 52-week highs—while Tesla is off 19.2%, Amazon 15.1%, and Nvidia 12.2%. Analysts said the results suggested that the entire sector was facing growing pains from the aggressive AI build-out. “The thinking is that these signs suggest that the entire sector is going to slow down,” said Chris Low of FHN Financial. The losses were compounded by a record-breaking $6.3 billion hack of cryptocurrency exchange Binance, which sent Bitcoin tumbling 5% to around $76,600 and dragged down crypto-related stocks such as Coinbase, Robinhood, and Strategy by more than 6% in premarket trading. Binance co-CEO Richard Teng said the exchange would cover all losses from its company funds. The exchange also said about $3 billion in assets had been frozen with the help of partners. Blockchain analysis firms linked the theft to North Korean hackers.

Adding to market pressure, oil prices surged on renewed geopolitical risks. Brent crude rose to $113 per barrel and West Texas Intermediate reached $104 per barrel after reports that the US may resume military strikes against Iran, threatening energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz. The yen strengthened against the dollar after the Bank of Japan held interest rates steady at 1.25% but revised up its inflation forecast, signaling readiness to continue raising borrowing costs. The dollar tracked Treasury yields lower as a fresh wave of selling in AI shares triggered a flight to safety.

stories.headline: Intel dives 29% as AI chip supply lags, PC market weak; Amazon slips 2%
body: Intel shares plummeted 29% on Friday, heading for their worst day since 1974, after the chipmaker issued weaker-than-expected guidance due to a plant shutdown in Israel and ongoing softness in the PC market. The stock was on pace for its second-steepest drop on record. Amazon shares also sold off, slipping about 1%, after the company reported a third-quarter miss on the top and bottom line while maintaining its capital expenditure forecast for 2026 of $220 billion. Amazon also reported negative free cash flow for the second consecutive quarter, and a big increase from the previous period. The Nasdaq Composite slid more than 2.5%, capping off a week of rough tech earnings.

Intel said it expects adjusted earnings per share of 25 cents this quarter on revenue between $15 billion and $16 billion. Analysts were expecting revenue of $17.1 billion and EPS of 43 cents, according to LSEG. The disappointing forecast reflects a PC market that's getting hammered due to soaring costs for memory and other components. Global PC shipments declined 4% in the second quarter from a year earlier, according to Counterpoint Research. Intel finance chief David Zinsner said in the release, 'We see the PC slowdown continuing at least through the first half of next year. We will continue making disciplined investments in capacity and working capital to increase supply and support future growth.'

The guidance also accounts for the effects of an explosion at a fab in Israel that killed two workers and seriously injured a third earlier this month. The incident will cost the company about $600 million in lost revenue over two quarters, Zinsner said. CEO Lip-Bu Tan, who was hired in March 2025, called the explosion an 'unfortunate and tragic accident' that caused an 'extended shutdown' at the plant, impacting shipments of 10-nanometer chips. Heading into Thursday's earnings report, Intel shares were up about 150% this year, buoyed by demand for central processors, which are becoming critical to agentic AI workloads.

Key to Tan's turnaround effort is Intel's foundry business, which has struggled to find its footing. Intel is the only U.S.-based manufacturer of advanced logic chips, and is now in high-volume production of its most advanced 18A chip out of its new fab in Arizona, providing an alternative to Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. Its next Arizona fab is expected to begin operations by the end of 2028. Intel still has no external customers for its new chips. 'We're going to have a couple of customers ready to announce the next two quarters,' Tan said on the call, adding that Intel is making 'tremendous progress' on its coming 14A chips.

Analysts at D.A. Davidson downgraded the stock to neutral from buy on Friday in a report titled 'Not fixed yet.' 'We understand the PC market is being impacted at the industry level,' the analysts wrote. 'However it is hard to justify the current multiple when weakness is so significant.' Other semiconductor names also notched declines. Chip giant Nvidia fell 4%, while Broadcom dropped about 6% and mobile chipmaker Qualcomm tumbled 12%. Alphabet on Thursday suffered its worst day on record, plunging more than 12%, and fell again on Friday.

Investors are growing nervous about the massive AI spending from the tech giants and whether their investments will pay off. Matt Orton, chief market strategist at Raymond James, told CNBC's 'Squawk Box Europe' on Friday, 'I don't think this is a moment of reckoning but I think it's a moment where investors should take a long thought about how positioning across the space still remains crowded even though the fundamentals are strong.'

stories.headline: Alphabet's record ~$500B wipeout sparks AI spending debate
body: Google parent Alphabet lost roughly $500 billion in market value Thursday, its worst day on record, after disappointing third-quarter earnings intensified investor concerns about the company's massive spending on artificial intelligence. Alphabet's Class A shares closed at $283.82, down 12.64%, erasing approximately $499.8 billion from the company's market capitalization — the second-largest single-day market value loss in stock market history.

The sell-off followed Alphabet's third-quarter report, released Wednesday, which showed revenue of $127.6 billion, up 25% from a year earlier but below Wall Street's expectation of $127.9 billion. Earnings of $2.67 per share were down 7% year over year and missed the $3.00 consensus — a double miss and the company's first since the fourth quarter of 2022, according to Kiplinger. Yahoo Finance noted that on a reported basis, per-share earnings slid to $2.12 from $2.87, with an $8.7 billion loss on equity securities cutting $0.55 from EPS and a year-earlier $10.7 billion gain adding $0.68; excluding those investment swings, earnings rose about 22% to roughly $2.67 from about $2.19. Operating income climbed 30% to $40.6 billion, or about 17% excluding last year's $3.5 billion European Commission fine.

The bigger worry for investors was the cost of Alphabet's AI buildout. The company spent approximately $51.4 billion on capital expenditures during the quarter — more than twice the year-ago total — with much of it directed at data centers and computing infrastructure. Free cash flow was negative for the second straight quarter, at $9.07 billion, and long-term debt jumped to $125.1 billion from $21.6 billion a year earlier. Alphabet maintained its full-year capex forecast of $195 billion to $205 billion, with spending projected to increase significantly again in 2027, and Chief Financial Officer Anat Ashkenazi warned that Google Cloud could face near-term pressure on profit margins as the company relies on outside computing capacity to meet demand.

The pressure to show returns on that spending is acute because growth in Alphabet's core search business is cooling: Google Search advertising revenue rose 12% from a year earlier, down from 17% growth in the prior quarter, as AI-powered search tools reshape the industry. Google Cloud, by contrast, was the standout. Cloud revenue more than doubled to $30.7 billion, up 103% and above analysts' estimate of $29.2 billion, marking the sixth straight quarter of accelerating growth. Cloud operating income roughly tripled to $11.1 billion, and the unit converted about 36% of revenue into operating profit, up from about 24% a year ago.

Analysts were divided on what the sell-off means. Wedbush's Ygal Arounian, who rates Alphabet Outperform, said the quarter-over-quarter slowdown in Search ad revenue growth "outweighs all other points in the print," but argued the company is "well positioned" and that Google "will prove a winner as AI advertising evolves." Seeking Alpha contended the post-earnings drop "looks increasingly mispriced." Alphabet shares had already fallen about 27% from their record close of $402.62 on May 13, Yahoo Finance noted. Thursday's loss surpassed Alphabet's previous record single-day market value decline of roughly $275 billion in July; Nvidia's $589 billion drop in January 2025 remains the largest on record.

The Alphabet rout weighed on the broader market. The Nasdaq Composite fell 1.4% to 26,184, the S&P 500 slipped 0.3% to 7,720, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 0.3% to 52,342. Caterpillar was the second-worst Dow stock, down 9.3% for its biggest one-day decline since March 2020, after third-quarter revenue of $20.7 billion (up 17% year over year) fell short of the $20.8 billion expected; earnings grew 45.5% to $7.20 per share. Oppenheimer analyst Kristen Owen noted strong sales across Caterpillar's businesses, led by 75% growth in its Power & Energy division — which supplies AI data centers — and said management expects moderate year-over-year growth in the fourth quarter.

Thursday's moves came as investors weighed fresh inflation data. The Federal Reserve's preferred gauge, the Personal Consumption Expenditures price index, rose 0.5% from August to September and was up 3.6% year over year; core PCE, excluding food and energy, rose 0.3% month over month and 3.1% year over year. "Although the inflation data came in line with expectations, because it is higher than the prior month, it emphasizes the problem we face — inflation is not coming down to the 2% target," said Chris Zaccarelli, chief investment officer at Northlight Asset Management. A separate report showed U.S. GDP grew 3.4% in the third quarter. Futures traders priced a 78% probability of a quarter-point Federal Reserve rate hike in December, down from 84% a day earlier.

stories.headline: U.S. GDP grows 3.4% in Q3 as inflation accelerates; Treasury yields near 5%
body: The U.S. economy expanded at a faster-than-expected annualized rate of 3.4% in the third quarter, the Commerce Department reported Thursday, surpassing the 3.1% consensus estimate and accelerating sharply from 2.2% in the second quarter. The better-than-expected growth was accompanied by a rise in the Federal Reserve’s preferred inflation gauge: the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index increased a seasonally adjusted 0.5% in September, putting the annual inflation rate at 3.6%, slightly below the 3.7% economists had forecast but still above the Fed’s 2% target. Excluding food and energy, the core PCE rose 0.3% for the month and 3.1% year-over-year, both in line with expectations.

Consumer spending climbed 0.5% in September (just below the 0.6% forecast) and rose 3.8% in the third quarter, matching the prior quarter’s pace. Gross private domestic investment surged 19.4%, fueled by a 20.9% jump in equipment spending and an 8.4% increase in intellectual property products. Real sales to private domestic purchasers—a proxy the Fed uses for underlying demand—rose 4.9% in the third quarter, up from 4.6% in the second quarter. Personal income increased 0.2% in September, slightly below the 0.3% estimate. Meanwhile, a separate Labor Department report showed initial jobless claims edged lower to a seasonally adjusted 194,000 for the week ended Oct. 24, below the 200,000 estimate and near levels last seen in the late 1960s.

September’s inflation acceleration was driven largely by a surge in energy costs: gasoline and other energy goods rose 9.2% for the month, while energy goods and services broadly jumped 5.4%. Services prices excluding energy and housing increased 0.4%, and housing costs rose 0.3%. On a quarterly basis, however, there was some encouraging news: headline PCE prices rose at a 2.1% annualized rate in the third quarter, and core PCE rose 2.5%, both down sharply from 5% and 3.3% in the second quarter. Economists cautioned that the monthly energy spike could be spreading to other parts of the economy.

The data arrived one day after the Federal Reserve voted to hold its benchmark interest rate in a range of 3.75% to 4%. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh told reporters Wednesday that policymakers are not on a preset course, saying, “If we had a firm conclusion about the conduct of monetary policy, we’d announce it to much fanfare today.” He described the coming period as “information rich” and said the Fed is keen to evaluate incoming data before deciding its next move. Markets are currently pricing in a more than 77% chance of a quarter-point rate hike in December, according to the CME’s FedWatch tool.

Following Thursday’s releases, stock market futures turned negative and Treasury yields fell. The yield on the 10-year Treasury—a benchmark for borrowing costs on mortgages and credit cards—hovered at 4.964%, more than 8 basis points lower on the day. The 2-year yield, which more closely tracks short-term Fed policy, lost more than 10 basis points to 4.629%, while the 30-year yield fell more than 5 basis points to 5.31%. “Net, net, economic growth is powering ahead despite the uncertainty of geopolitical risks and the damage posed to many sectors of the economy by higher energy costs,” said Chris Rupkey, chief economist at Fwdbonds. “The economy was thought to have been a lost cause during much of the current Administration's time in office, but real GDP has bounced back above a 3 percent run rate in Q3 2026 for the first time in a year.”

Analysts said the data is unlikely to change the Fed’s overall assessment. Stephen Coltman, head of macro at 21shares, noted that Warsh sees the economy as strong, inflation above target, and financial conditions as not currently restrictive, and that “today's data will not change that overall assessment and investors should expect the Fed Funds rate to continue to rise as a result.” Ali Hassan, a portfolio manager at Thornburg Investment Management, said markets initially viewed the Fed’s October statement as “a softer policy path, not an inflation scare,” but cautioned that the test will come Friday, when the blackout on Fed policymakers’ additional commentary lifts. “If Fed speakers put more hikes back on the table, they could claw back the front-end easing and blunt the self-defeating dynamic,” Hassan said.

stories.headline: Exxon, Chevron, BP beat estimates on refining margins; oil majors rally
stories.byline: Financial & Markets desk · anchored on Reuters
body: ExxonMobil and Chevron delivered third-quarter earnings that topped analyst expectations, driven by a surge in refining margins as geopolitical conflicts disrupted fuel production. ExxonMobil reported adjusted earnings per share of $4.23, above the Bloomberg consensus estimate of $4.13, while Chevron posted adjusted earnings of $5.28 per share versus the $4.88 forecast. Chevron’s revenue rose 36% year over year to $67.8 billion, exceeding the $60.55 billion consensus, and its U.S. refineries achieved record crude throughput of 1.09 million barrels per day with utilization rates near 98%. The strong results lifted shares across the sector, with Chevron stock gaining 2.2% following the report.

The earnings beats were largely attributed to higher refining margins, which ExxonMobil said would add roughly $4.5 billion to its overall results after a $4.1 billion boost in the prior quarter. The margin increases were triggered by ongoing wars in the Middle East and Ukraine, which have disrupted activity at critical fuel-producing facilities and caused prices for diesel and gasoline to spike. The returns echoed similarly solid profits at other Western oil groups such as Shell and TotalEnergies, underscoring a broad trend among integrated oil majors benefiting from the conflict-driven environment.

The strong quarterly performance comes during a broader earnings season in which nearly a quarter of S&P 500 companies have reported, with an overall earnings growth rate of 29.5%. If that rate holds, it would mark the third straight quarter of earnings growth above 25%. For the oil majors, the results reflect the continued impact of twin conflicts — the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine — on global energy markets.

Investors responded positively to the results, with Chevron shares rising in premarket trading and ExxonMobil stock also gaining. The sector’s rally signals confidence that the favorable margin environment may persist, though analysts will be watching for any easing of geopolitical tensions or shifts in refinery utilization that could alter the outlook. For now, the integrated oil giants have delivered a clear demonstration of how refining operations can serve as a powerful earnings driver during periods of supply disruption.

stories.headline: Pulisic signs AC Milan deal through 2031
body: AC Milan announced Friday that American forward Christian Pulisic has signed a contract extension keeping him at the club through June 30, 2031. The new deal adds four years to his previous contract, which was set to expire in the summer of 2027. Pulisic joined AC Milan in July 2023 from Chelsea for approximately $20 million.

In its announcement, AC Milan said Pulisic has established himself as a key member of the team since arriving, highlighting his technical ability, character, consistency and work ethic. The club noted that he has scored 44 goals in 141 appearances for the Rossoneri, underscoring his importance to the squad and his role in the club's future plans. The extension reflects a shared commitment to building on progress made together and achieving new milestones.

Pulisic's time in Serie A has included both highs and lows. He became an immediate key player under Stefano Pioli but faced challenges adapting to different tactical systems under a series of managers — Pioli, Paulo Fonseca, Sergio Conceicao, Massimiliano Allegri and current coach Ruben Amorim. Recurring injuries have forced him to miss significant playing time over the past two years, and the new deal is seen as a chance for greater stability on the pitch.

When fit, Pulisic has proven himself one of Serie A's best performers, and both his coach and teammates rely on his presence. That reliability was a major reason AC Milan, under American owner Gerry Cardinale, chose to extend his contract. In the summer of 2026, when the club underwent changes in management and coaching, Amorim and Cardinale agreed that Pulisic should be a key part of the new cycle, which they hope will bring trophies and lead into the 2031-32 season, when AC Milan plans to move into a new stadium unveiled jointly with city rivals Inter on Thursday. The announcement came ahead of Saturday's Derby della Madonnina against Inter at San Siro.

stories.headline: MLB lockout looms as labor deal expires Dec. 1; salary cap at center of fight
body: Major League Baseball's 2027 season is threatened by a looming lockout, with the current five-year collective bargaining agreement set to expire on Dec. 1. The last game of the 2026 season, in which the Milwaukee Brewers clinched their first World Series title, could be the final one played for an extended period. Owners have proposed a salary cap for the first time since a 1994 proposal led to a 232-day strike that wiped out the playoffs and World Series, and both sides are digging in for a protracted battle.

Management is pushing for a salary cap and floor to reduce payroll disparity, along with a restriction limiting any single player to 15% of a team's payroll. The players, who have opposed a cap for decades, are seeking expanded free agency and salary arbitration rights, nearly doubling the major league minimum, increasing revenue sharing from high-revenue teams, and imposing a tax on teams that fail to maintain payroll at a certain level. Interim union chief Bruce Meyer has likened a salary cap to "a nuclear bomb," and player representatives describe negotiations as "worthless" and a "charade," with no back-and-forth on core economics.

The sides have been negotiating since May but have found no common ground. The expectation, based on past statements from Commissioner Rob Manfred, is that owners will authorize a lockout when the deal expires. The last lockout, in 2021-22, lasted 99 days and ended on March 10, forcing a truncated spring training and a compressed 162-game season. This time, with a salary cap on the table, the fight could be more protracted. Talks historically do not intensify until the threat of missing regular-season games looms in late February or early March.

The looming lockout is already shaping the offseason. Teams face a flurry of deadlines before Dec. 1, including the Nov. 17 deadline for free agents to accept or decline qualifying offers and the Nov. 20 non-tender deadline. The 2021-22 lockout created a free-agent frenzy before the expiration, with clubs committing $1.4 billion in salaries on Dec. 1, 2021. This year's free-agent class is headlined by Tarik Skubal, Freddy Peralta, Michael King, Seiya Suzuki and Randy Arozarena, with 144 new free agents as of Thursday and dozens more expected by Monday.

Players have been preparing for a lockout and a fight on a cap for years. The union's executive subcommittee, which includes holdover Marcus Semien from the 2021-22 talks and newer members such as Chris Bassitt and Paul Skenes, has worked to keep all 30 teams united. "We have made massive, massive strides in just educating players, keeping players together," Bassitt said. "Now it's all 30 teams pulling from the same rope." Owners, meanwhile, say they are united on their cap plan, which MLB argues would benefit the majority of players who make close to the minimum—about 40% of players on 40-man rosters at season's end had less than one year of service.

The stakes are enormous for a nearly $13 billion industry. Commissioner Manfred has cited a $441 million gap between the highest and lowest payrolls as evidence of competitive imbalance, saying it "defies human experience" to ask fans to believe both ends have the same chance to win. With no deal expected by the Dec. 1 deadline, the sport faces a deep freeze that will impact when next season begins and could threaten the scheduled March 24 start date.

stories.headline: Snakebite crisis kills up to 513,000 people a year, study finds
body: A startling new study suggests that venomous snakebites are killing far more people worldwide than official statistics indicate, with an estimated 274,000 to 513,000 deaths every year. Researchers found that as many as 7 million people could suffer snake envenoming annually, while more than 800,000 survivors are left with long-term disabilities. The findings update a milestone 2008 global burden study and reveal a hidden public health crisis.

Snake envenoming occurs when venom is injected into the body through a bite, and it mostly affects poor rural communities across tropical and subtropical regions who lack easy access to medical care. Over half of the countries where venomous snakes pose a threat do not keep count of how many people are bitten or envenomed. In rural sub-Saharan Africa and south Asia, many victims live hours away from the nearest clinic, lack transport, or seek care from traditional healers, so their cases are never captured in national health statistics.

To bridge this massive data gap, the researchers looked at data from 79 countries by reviewing studies published up to March 31, 2025. They built a geostatistical model that combines real-world data with local environmental and socioeconomic factors, including climate, snake species richness, and socioeconomic indicators. The model calculates the probability of snakebites occurring in specific locations, even where official health records are completely blank, and produces both a baseline floor and a potential upper ceiling for envenomings and fatalities.

The geographic distribution of the burden is uneven. Sub-Saharan Africa alone accounts for 45% of all global envenomings and fatalities, and people there experience snake envenoming and death at nearly three times the rate seen in south Asia. Countries like Nigeria, the Democratic Republic of Congo, and Ethiopia face a high burden, driven by dense rural populations and high exposure in agricultural fields. The continent hosts a rich diversity of medically important venomous species, including saw-scaled vipers, puff adders, African cobras, and mambas. Fragile health systems, long travel distances, and the high cost or absence of effective antivenom mean a treatable medical emergency can quickly become fatal.

The World Health Organization has set an ambitious target to halve snakebite mortality and disability by 2030. The researchers say that mapping the problem at the country level is the first crucial step. By identifying high-risk hotspots, governments and global health partners can strategically stockpile antivenom where it is needed most, train primary healthcare workers in high-burden rural zones, and improve rapid transport infrastructure. As the authors note, better data cannot solve the problem alone, but can help ensure that antivenom, healthcare services, and prevention efforts reach the communities that need them most.

stories.headline: Binance loses $6.3 billion in record crypto heist blamed on North Korea
body: Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, suspended all deposits and withdrawals Friday after hackers stole roughly $6.3 billion in digital assets, in what security researchers called the largest cryptocurrency heist on record. The exchange put the "estimated total impact" of the attack at about $6.3 billion and said around $3 billion of the affected assets — mainly stablecoins that act as cash for the crypto market — had been frozen by industry partners. Blockchain intelligence firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis attributed the theft to TraderTraitor, a North Korean cybercrime cell focused on stealing cryptocurrency.

Binance said its initial investigation indicated that attackers compromised a DevOps engineer's laptop, which "allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions." In a subsequent update, the company said the investigation "has uncovered additional points of breach," and co-CEO Richard Teng said the attack was not a "one-click" action but a more complex process. Binance said it found no evidence of a leak of its wallet private keys. Blockchain analytics firm Elliptic estimated that the attacker converted about $3.3 billion of the stolen assets into digital currencies that cannot be frozen and was working to cash those out as traditional money.

TRM said most of the theft occurred in just 20 minutes, making it roughly four times larger than the previous record, when about $1.46 billion was taken from exchange Bybit last year in a heist also blamed on North Korean hackers. Elliptic, which also tied the Binance theft to North Korea, said some of the stolen funds ended up in the same wallet used in an earlier cyberattack on crypto exchange Bitget this year, when hackers stole $351 million. The hack escalates a wave of large-scale crypto thefts that followed several heists disclosed in September, prompting new concerns about the industry's exposure to sophisticated attackers.

Binance said "user funds are completely safe" and publicly committed to covering all losses from the breach. The company, which says it holds about $140 billion in digital assets, said it had reserved more than $6.34 billion of company funds to cover the incident — with $5 billion already held in the exact token assets that were impacted — and was buying more tokens to make up the remainder. It also maintains an emergency reserve fund of around $1.3 billion. During the response, Tether froze about $1.56 billion related to the hack and Circle froze roughly $800 million in Tether as it moved through its networks.

Early estimates before Binance's disclosure had suggested at least $2 billion was drained from the exchange's hot wallets, with some unconfirmed estimates as high as $5.7 billion. The incident is a major blow to Binance, co-founded in 2017 by Changpeng Zhao, who said he expects user funds to be "fully covered" but gave no explanation. Zhao's company in 2023 pleaded guilty to U.S. criminal charges for breaching anti-money-laundering laws and paid a $4.3 billion fine; Binance was also hacked in 2019, losing $40 million. North Korea, which remains cut off from the global financial system over its nuclear weapons program, has long used crypto theft to fund it. Peter Ward of the Sejong Institute in Seoul said the country offers "near-total protection to its hackers." "Things may get a lot worse going forward," he said.

TRM chief policy officer Ari Redbord said, "This is an extraordinary hack, for its size and for the response... Few financial systems have ever shown a theft of this scale." The breach raises questions about how a single employee's laptop could reach systems controlling billions of dollars, and whether Binance had recently undergone a third-party security audit; the company did not respond to requests on those points. Binance said it will publish an updated proof of reserves once remediation is complete and continues to work with law enforcement to trace, freeze, and recover funds. In a separate incident Thursday, prediction market Polymarket briefly halted trading after hackers stole about $2 million in user funds by compromising software from a company called DebugBear. The heist also follows an OpenAI report that one of its AI models swiped fake crypto on an Ethereum test network, adding to concerns about how AI tools could be used maliciously against the industry.

stories.headline: GM to pay $220 million to 36 states over selling driver data to insurers
body: General Motors will pay $220 million to settle allegations from a coalition of 36 states that it illegally sold private driving behavior and location information to data brokers, which then passed the data to insurance providers, according to agreements announced Thursday. The settlement, reached with the District of Columbia and 35 states that had sued the automaker, also requires GM to obtain drivers' express consent before collecting or sharing their driving and location data, and to have a third party independently assess the company's compliance with its privacy program.

The dispute centered on GM's Smart Driver system, a free feature inside its connected car apps that tracked and rated driving behaviors, including seat belt use, and which GM marketed as a way for parents to monitor teen drivers or for adults to track their own driving habits. In 2024, however, reports emerged that GM and its OnStar subsidiary had shared that data with brokers such as LexisNexis and Verisk, who in turn sold it to insurance companies. Some drivers found their insurance rates increased as a result, and many said they had no knowledge of ever agreeing to share such data for those purposes.

GM discontinued Smart Driver in 2024, but legal action continued. In January, the Federal Trade Commission finalized an order banning GM and OnStar from sharing geolocation data or driver behavior data with third parties for five years, a settlement the companies entered last year. The new multistate agreement follows the same terms as those previous settlements with California and the FTC, but adds the requirement for third-party verification of GM's compliance rather than relying on the company's own word.

In a statement, GM said: 'Safer, more helpful and personalized experiences are enabled by connected vehicle data, and GM is committed to being clear about what information is used, how it's protected, and the choices customers have about what they share.' The company also said the agreement addresses Smart Driver, 'a product we ended in 2024, and reinforces steps we've taken to strengthen our privacy practices.' GM said it will no longer sell vehicle information that can be linked to an individual, their vehicle location, or how they drive, though it may still disclose anonymized data not tied to an individual with certain partners. The company has updated its privacy policy and created a consumer-facing Privacy Center.

GM, for example, is adding a personal AI assistant to OnStar, its 30-year-old safety and roadside assistance service, with vehicle cameras connected to software for live views and crash recordings, plus voice controls for functions like climate. When GM announced that assistant in October, it emphasized privacy protections: customers can decide what data is shared, recordings have time limits and are encrypted, and GM and OnStar cannot access Connected Camera recordings. Still, GM said customers who opt not to share data will likely have limited access to certain features.
